title: Blood Products Reference
sources: Critical Vector — 6 Blood Products You Must Know Cold (verified vs AABB 2023 RBC + 2025 AABB/ICTMG platelet guidelines)
Carson JL et al. Red Blood Cell Transfusion: 2023 AABB International Guidelines. JAMA 2023;330(19):1892-1902
Metcalf RA et al. Platelet Transfusion: 2025 AABB & ICTMG Guidelines. JAMA 2025;334(7):606-617
Critical Vector — Fibrinogen Concentrate vs Cryoprecipitate; CRYOSTAT-2, JAMA 2023 (n=1,604)

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV blood-products guide + the fibrinogen-concentrate-vs-cryoprecipitate decision guide. AABB thresholds verified exact.

summary: Indication, constituents, effect, and the clock on each of the six core products, plus the fibrinogen-concentrate-vs-cryoprecipitate decision. AABB restrictive RBC thresholds: 7 g/dL general, 7.5 cardiac surgery, 8 orthopedic surgery / known CVD. Platelet thresholds (2025 AABB/ICTMG): 10 prophylaxis, 50 major surgery, 100 neuro/posterior-eye.

rows: Packed red cells (PRBC)
Symptomatic anemia. Transfuse below Hb 7 g/dL (general), 7.5 (cardiac surgery), 8 (orthopedic surgery or known CVD)
Red cells in preservative; no platelets, no clotting factors. 1 unit → Hb ~ +1 g/dL, Hct ~ +3%
Start within 30 min of issue, complete within 4 h; store 1–6 °C. ABO + Rh compatible, cross-matched.
Platelets
Prophylaxis below 10 ×10⁹/L if non-bleeding (hypoproliferative — chemo, allo-SCT). Procedures: below 50 for major non-neuraxial surgery, below 100 for neurosurgery / posterior-eye
1 adult pool or apheresis unit → count ~ +30–50 ×10⁹/L
20–24 °C with continuous agitation, NOT refrigerated; 5-day shelf life (7 if pathogen-reduced); transfuse over 30–60 min. Do NOT give for cardiac bypass or spontaneous ICH without active bleeding.
Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
Bleeding with multiple factor deficiency (massive transfusion, DIC, liver disease); TTP plasma exchange
All coagulation factors ~ 1 IU/mL incl. labile V and VIII. Dose 10–15 mL/kg → factor levels ~ +20%
Once thawed, use within 24 h at 1–6 °C. ABO-compatible (opposite convention to red cells). NOT first-line for warfarin reversal if PCC is available.
Cryoprecipitate
Fibrinogen < 1.5 g/L with bleeding (DIC, massive transfusion); < 2 g/L in obstetric hemorrhage
Fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII, vWF, fibronectin. Per unit ≥ 150 mg fibrinogen + ≥ 80 IU factor VIII; a 10-unit adult pool → fibrinogen ~ +1 g/L
Once thawed, use within 6 h (4 h if open-pooled), room temperature, not refrigerated. NOT for warfarin reversal. It is a fibrinogen concentrate, not 'concentrated plasma'.
Whole blood (LTOWB)
Trauma / massive hemorrhage resuscitation
Red cells + plasma + cold-stored platelets together; group O, low anti-A/anti-B titer; ~ 500 mL, leukoreduced with a platelet-sparing filter
Start within 30 min of issue, complete within 4 h; store 1–6 °C; 21-day (CPD) / 35-day (CPDA-1) shelf life. Cold-stored platelet function falls after ~ 14 days though red cells + plasma stay usable.
Prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC)
Urgent warfarin reversal with major bleeding, or before emergency surgery
Factors II, VII, IX, X + proteins C and S. Dose 25–50 IU/kg, INR-based; ALWAYS co-give IV vitamin K. Corrects INR within ~ 10–30 min
Plasma-derived factor concentrate, not a cellular component — low volume, minimal TACO risk vs FFP. Main risk is thrombosis. 3-factor PCC lacks factor VII and is not equivalent for warfarin reversal.

body.text: The 80 ×10⁹/L platelet figure for neuraxial / epidural procedures is a long-standing anesthesia-specific convention — distinct from the 2025 AABB/ICTMG hematology threshold of 20 ×10⁹/L for a diagnostic lumbar puncture. They answer different questions (one-off LP vs an indwelling epidural catheter), so they don't match when looked up side by side.

items: The clock starts the moment a unit leaves controlled storage.
The 30-minute rule: a unit out of controlled storage for more than 30 minutes usually cannot return to stock.
Right product, right patient, right dose, right time, right documentation — two-person bedside check, every time.

body.text: Fibrinogen (Factor I) is the substrate for the fibrin clot and the first coagulation factor to fall critically low in massive, trauma, and obstetric hemorrhage. Target 1.5–2.0 g/L during active bleeding (a level ~ 2.3 g/L is associated with the lowest mortality). FFP alone cannot correct severe hypofibrinogenemia without unacceptable volume. Viscoelastic trigger: ROTEM FIBTEM A5 < 8 mm or A10 < 10 mm (or the TEG functional-fibrinogen equivalent).

rows: Dosing
Standardized ~ 1 g/vial; usual dose 3–6 g
Variable fibrinogen per unit/pool; 10–20 units (0.5–1 L) raise fibrinogen ~ 0.6–1.2 g/L
Volume
Low — ~ 50 mL/vial
Large — greater volume-overload risk
Logistics
Reconstitution needed; no ABO testing; may not be on formulary
Widely available; 20–30 min thaw (unless a pre-thawed protocol exists); multi-donor exposure
Extras
Fibrinogen only
Also contains factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII, fibronectin
Cost
Higher acquisition cost in most systems
Lower direct cost

items: Choose FC when rapid correction is needed and it's on formulary, precise weight-based dosing is required, ABO type is unknown with expected delays, or the patient is volume-sensitive (heart / renal failure).
Choose cryo when FC is unavailable or off-formulary, cost is a constraint, additional factor deficiencies (vWF, FVIII, FXIII) are suspected, or a pre-thawed cryo protocol removes the thaw delay.

CRYOSTAT-2 (JAMA 2023, n = 1,604 trauma): empiric early cryoprecipitate vs standard care — no 28-day mortality difference (25.3% vs 26.1%). Empiric early cryo in unselected trauma does not improve survival.

Curry SR/MA (Br J Anaesth 2022): evidence sparse and high risk of bias; insufficient to establish clear superiority of either product. Fibrinogen is the first to fall and the first to replace — the product matters less than the speed.
